newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bank of France member slams devaluation message.
newsitem.headline: Bank of France member slams devaluation message.

text.p: A member of the Bank of France's inner circle of policymakers rejected calls for a devalued franc on Sunday, saying it would be economically wrong, politically impossible and might blow single currency plans off course.

Jean Boissonnat, who sits on the central bank's monetary policy council, wrote in a newspaper that a currency devaluation proposed by former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing last week was not the unemployment cure he thought.
And he took an unusually fierce swipe at the co-founder of Europe's current monetary system, saying some had written off his intervention as the actions of a frustrated child.

"We all know children who break their toys to protest against the fact they are not getting enough attention," were Boissonnat's opening words in a front-page piece in the weekly Journal du Dimanche, published on Sunday.
"Any devaluation means national impoverishment," Boissonnat said. "It is only justified as a penalty for bad management."
Giscard d'Estaing, writing in the weekly magazine L'Express on Wednesday, said a lower franc was needed to breathe life into the French economy and create jobs.

The veteran centrist's views fuelled a debate about a decade-old "strong franc" policy in France, with some Eurosceptic right-wingers outside government backing devaluation and France and Germany issuing a rare joint statement to defend the rate between their two currencies as jitters hit the franc.

Although Giscard d'Estaing said afterwards he was mainly talking about lowering the franc against the dollar, his article said this would likely correspond to a weaker franc against the mark, the central pair in Europe's single currency project.
Boissonnat said devaluing the franc against the mark had no economic justification because France's competitive position against Germany had improved over the past decade.
This was because both prices and pay had risen more quickly in Germany than in France, while the central rate between the two currencies in Europe's monetary grid had not altered.
Without good economic reasons, devaluation would be politically impossible because France's partners in the European Monetary System would have to agree on any changes, he said.
Other countries would simply point at France's 100 billion franc ($19.65 billion) surplus as proof it was still competitive.
If France then insisted on lowering its currency, it could see its single currency dreams shattered.
"If we wanted to lower the franc against the mark despite this opposition, we would have to leave the EMS, which means renouncing a single currency," he said.
French and German involvement is widely seen as the linchpin of plans to introduce a common currency, the euro, in 1999.

Boissonnat said the notion that devaluation was good for jobs was disproved by the facts: employment had dropped five percent in Italy since the lira dropped out of the managed Exchange Rate Mechanism of the EMS in 1992.
Finance ministers were meeting in Brussels later on Sunday to try to iron out differences over Italy's re-entry to the ERM.

Boissonnat said it was true Europe as a whole had suffered from the dollar being undervalued in recent years. But the United States had been able to escape the costs of a weaker currency in higher interest rates, because savers had no other superpower-sized market to turn to for their investments.

"It is precisely in to contest this privilege that Europe wants to unify its currencies," he said. Doing so would create a large market for capital inside Europe, helping to lower interest rates and promote employment.
He said Franco-German debates still existed over the way to manage the future euro, however.
"These debates are going on and they are real," he wrote. "We certainly don't advance them by making verbal flourishes or seeking advantage in front of photographers." ($1=5.088 French Franc)
